| **5.1.1** | Verify that the application has defenses against HTTP parameter pollution attacks, particularly if the application framework makes no distinction about the source of request parameters (GET, POST, cookies, headers, or environment variables). | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 235 |

There are no such things as GET or POST parameters, those are HTTP methods. We should use URL parameters and message body instead.

comments.body: @elarlang do environment variables have anything to do with parameter pollution? Not sure I can think of any link...
Good point Josh. I think the answer is no, this is a framework issue from what I see.

There are some very loose association's.

1. Indirect Link Through Misconfiguration or Poor Practices:
Poor handling of environment variables (e.g., improper use or leakage) could lead to vulnerabilities or be exploited in parameter pollution attacks if, for example, environment variables are used to control aspects of input validation or are inadvertently exposed to the user.

2. Injection Attacks: In scenarios where environment variables are used in constructing responses to user inputs or configuring how user inputs are handled, improper validation or sanitation of these inputs could lead to injection attacks. Though not parameter pollution per se, it shares the underlying theme of exploiting improperly handled user input.

I still think these are fairly weak associations...

Maybe there are some PHP superglobal vibes here. With that (mis)configuration it is actually a thing.
* https://www.php.net/manual/en/language.variables.superglobals.php
* https://www.php.net/manual/en/reserved.variables.globals.php

I humbly suggest "has defenses against ~~HTTP~~ parameter and body pollution attacks" and remove "environment variables" from this requirement. I would say that if a client-side environment variable gets passed, it's a parameter/body variable. If an environment variable is used on the server side, it would be a configuration issue.

"parameter and body" are so wide terms, and without context (HTTP) it is not understandable. We need to keep the term HTTP parameter pollution, as it is a known attack, and name or describe the problem in other words.

I accepted the PR, but I reopen the issue - do we need or can anyone recommend additional improvement here?
| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **5.1.1** | [MODIFIED] Verify that the application has defenses against HTTP parameter pollution attacks, particularly if the application framework makes no distinction about the source of request parameters (query string, body parameters, cookies, headers, or environment variables). | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 235 |

And is it actually input validation problem? Or should belong to current 10.4 together with requirement:
_V10.4.1 [ADDED] Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations to avoid type juggling or confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type._
HTTP parameter pollution is definitely an input validation problem, not a type juggling confusion vulnerability.
Opened #1883 to fix the env var thing
Just want to ask if we have a requirement in v14 Config chapter that covers for the HTTP environment variables (e.g. GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) if those were tampered in the HTTP requests?
Not sure I understand @csfreak92, can you check and if not open a new issue?
